name: Yumo Mikyö Dorje (yu mo mi bskyod rdo rje)
summary: Eleventh-century Tibetan Kālacakra master, counted by the Jonang as the first Tibetan in their lineage of the six-branch yoga; a student of the Kashmiri paṇḍita Somanātha; the Four Clear Lamps are attributed to him.

name: Somanātha (zla ba mgon po), the Kashmiri paṇḍita
alt_names: kha che zla ba mgon po
summary: Kashmiri paṇḍita who brought the Kālacakra teaching to Tibet in the 11th century and, with the translator Dro Lotsawa Sherab Drak, stands at the head of the Dro transmission from which the Jonang lineage derives.

name: Künpang Thukje Tsöndrü (kun spangs thugs rje brtson 'grus)
summary: Founder of the Jonang hermitage in the Jomonang valley (c. 1294); a Kālacakra adept who is said to have received and unified seventeen transmission lines of the six-branch yoga, from which the Jonang takes its name and practice lineage.

name: Changsem Gyalwa Yeshe (byang sems rgyal ba ye shes)
summary: Künpang Thukje Tsöndrü's successor at Jonang in the Kālacakra lineage.

name: Khetsün Yönten Gyatso (mkhas btsun yon tan rgya mtsho) of Jonang
summary: Abbot of Jonang before Dolpopa and Dolpopa's principal teacher of the Kālacakra six-branch yoga.

name: Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen (dol po pa shes rab rgyal mtshan)
places: Lhasa and central Tibet (teaching journey late in life)

realization_account.text: The Jonang account holds that the other-emptiness view dawned in Dolpopa's own experience through the six-branch yoga before he set it out in writing, and that he was an emanation of the Kalkī Puṇḍarīka, author of the Vimalaprabhā (emanation claim: low confidence).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great systematizer of the Jonang and of the other-emptiness (gzhan stong) view. Born in Dolpo, he trained at Sakya, received the Kālacakra six-branch yoga at Jonang, became its abbot, built its great stūpa, oversaw a new translation of the Kālacakra tantra and Vimalaprabhā, and taught — in the Mountain Doctrine, the Fourth Council and many other works — that the ultimate, buddha-nature, is permanent and empty only of what is other than it. Known as 'the Omniscient One of Dolpo'.

name: Sabzang Mati Paṇchen Lodrö Gyaltsen (sa bzang ma ti paN chen blo gros rgyal mtshan)
summary: Disciple of Dolpopa and co-translator, with Jonang Lotsawa Lodrö Pal, of the Jonang revision of the Kālacakra tantra and Vimalaprabhā; also a commentator on the Kālacakra.

name: Jonang Lotsawa Lodrö Pal (jo nang lo tsA ba blo gros dpal)
summary: Translator in Dolpopa's circle who, with Mati Paṇchen, prepared the Jonang translation of the Kālacakra tantra and the Vimalaprabhā.

name: Bodong Chogle Namgyal (bo dong phyogs las rnam rgyal)
summary: Disciple of Dolpopa who succeeded to the Jonang seat and was a prolific Kālacakra scholar.

name: Nyabön Kunga Pal (nya dbon kun dga' dpal)
summary: A student of Dolpopa who upheld the other-emptiness teaching and taught widely in central Tibet.

name: Jetsün Kunga Drolchok (rje btsun kun dga' grol mchog)
summary: Sixteenth-century Jonang master, compiler of the hundred and eight Jonang instructions (khrid brgya); Tāranātha was recognized as his rebirth.

name: Tāranātha (Jetsün Kunga Nyingpo, rje btsun kun dga' snying po)

realization_account.text: Regarded as the rebirth of Kunga Drolchok; after his death he was recognized as reborn in Mongolia as Zanabazar, the first Jebtsundamba Khutughtu.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great reviver of the Jonang: recognized as the rebirth of Kunga Drolchok, he received the Kālacakra, the Shangpa instructions and, from the Indian yogin Buddhaguptanātha, the seven instruction lineages; wrote on other-emptiness (The Essence of Other-Emptiness, Twenty-one Differences), on Kālacakra practice (Meaningful to Behold), and histories of Indian Buddhism and of the Tārā tantra; and founded Takten Phuntsok Ling (1615). Soon after his death his seats were converted to Gelug.

name: Buddhaguptanātha
summary: An Indian yogin and traveller of the 16th century from whom Tāranātha received the seven instruction lineages and many siddha transmissions (the tradition's account).

name: Öndör Gegeen Zanabazar, the first Jebtsundamba Khutughtu

realization_account.text: Recognized as the rebirth of Tāranātha.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Mongolian lama and artist, first of the Jebtsundamba incarnations; in the tradition's account the rebirth of Tāranātha, which links the Jonang line of incarnation to Mongolia.

name: Bamda Gelek Gyatso ('ba' mda' dge legs rgya mtsho)
summary: Jonang scholar of Amdo, a prolific writer on Kālacakra and other-emptiness in the surviving eastern tradition.

name: Ngawang Lodrö Drakpa (ngag dbang blo gros grags pa)
summary: Twentieth-century Jonang master of Dzamthang and author of the history of the Jonang tradition.

name: Butön Rinchen Drub (bu ston rin chen grub)
notes: Usually counted as founder of the Zhalu (Bulug) tradition; no separate lineage id used here.
summary: Scholar of Zhalu, compiler of the Tibetan canon (Kangyur/Tengyur catalogues) and a leading Kālacakra master, contemporary of Dolpopa; his treatise on the tathāgatagarbha reads the buddha-nature teaching as of provisional meaning, against the other-emptiness reading.

name: Machig Labdrön (ma gcig lab sgron)
alt_names: Machig Lapkyi Drönma (ma gcig lab kyi sgron ma)

realization_account.text: She is an emanation of the Great Mother Prajñāpāramitā and of Tārā; in her previous life she was an Indian paṇḍita (named Mönlam Drub in the accounts, low confidence) whose consciousness passed to Tibet; she attained realization while reading the chapter on māras in the Perfection of Wisdom; Indian scholars who came to test her accepted her teaching and carried Chöd to India.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tibetan woman master (11th–12th c.) who founded the Chöd practice lineage. A gifted reciter of the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras, she realized their meaning while reading, received instructions from Kyotön Sönam Lama and from Padampa Sangye, married the Indian yogin Thöpa Bhadra, raised children who became lineage holders, and taught at Zangri Khangmar. Her Great Bundle of Precepts is the root text of Chöd.

name: Padampa Sangye (pha dam pa sangs rgyas)

realization_account.text: A siddha who studied with a great number of Indian masters (fifty-four in one account); some Tibetan accounts identify him with earlier Indian figures (low confidence; not recorded here).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: South Indian siddha who made several visits to Tibet (five or seven in different accounts), founded the Pacification (zhi byed) tradition, gave instructions to Machig Labdrön that became the 'father' strand of Chöd, and spent his last years at Dingri, where he gave his Hundred Verses to the people of Dingri.

name: Āryadeva the Brahmin (bram ze Ārya de ba)
summary: An Indian master to whom the Chöd tradition attributes the Grand Poem on the Perfection of Wisdom; treated as an Indian source of Chöd. Distinct from Nāgārjuna's disciple Āryadeva in most accounts (identity uncertain).

name: Kyotön Sönam Lama (skyo ston bsod nams bla ma)
summary: Machig Labdrön's principal teacher, who gave her empowerment and instruction; a holder of Padampa Sangye's teachings.

name: Thöpa Bhadra (thod pa bha dra)
summary: Indian yogin who became Machig Labdrön's consort; their union is presented in her biography as foretold.

name: Gyalwa Döndrub (rgyal ba don grub)
summary: Son of Machig Labdrön and a holder of her Chöd lineage; several teachings in the Complete Explanation are framed as answers to his questions (low confidence).

name: Tönyön Samdrub (thod smyon bsam grub)
summary: A son (in some accounts a grandson) of Machig Labdrön, holder of the family lineage of Chöd.

name: Dampa Kunga (dam pa kun dga')
summary: Principal Tibetan disciple of Padampa Sangye at Dingri and holder of the later transmission of Pacification.

name: Bhaiṣajyaguru, the Medicine Buddha (sangs rgyas sman bla)

realization_account.text: A buddha whose twelve vows (Bhaiṣajyaguru sūtra) include healing all beings.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: In Sowa Rigpa the teacher of the Four Tantras: seated in the medicine city Tanaduk, he emanates the sage Rigpé Yeshe, who teaches, and Yilé Kyé, who requests. Physicians practise his sādhana and consecrate medicines in his name.

name: Rigpé Yeshe (rig pa'i ye shes), the sage 'Awareness-Wisdom'
summary: The emanation of the Medicine Buddha's mind who teaches the Four Tantras (the tradition's account).

name: Yilé Kyé (yid las skyes), the sage 'Born from Mind'
summary: The emanation of the Medicine Buddha's speech who requests the Four Tantras and records them (the tradition's account).

name: Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Elder (g.yu thog rnying ma yon tan mgon po)

scholarly.text: historicity doubted; the figure may be a later projection of the Younger

realization_account.text: An emanation of the Medicine Buddha; lived 125 years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: In the tradition's account the chief physician of King Trisong Detsen, who travelled to India and elsewhere to study, received the Four Tantras from Vairocana and lived to a great age; regarded as an emanation of the Medicine Buddha. Scholars question his historicity.

name: Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger (g.yu thog gsar ma yon tan mgon po)
summary: Twelfth-century physician, in the tradition's account the thirteenth-generation descendant of the Elder, who revised the Four Tantras into their present form (in the scholarly account, compiled them) and is the source of the Yuthok Nyingthig, the physicians' spiritual practice.

name: Drapa Ngönshé (grwa pa mngon shes)
summary: Treasure revealer who, in the tradition's account, recovered the Four Tantras in 1038 from a pillar of the main temple at Samye.

name: Sumtön Yeshe Zung (sum ston ye shes gzungs)
summary: Principal disciple of Yuthok the Younger, through whom the Yuthok Nyingthig and the Four Tantras lineage were passed on.

name: Jangdak Namgyal Drakzang (byang bdag rnam rgyal grags bzang)
summary: Lord of Jang Ngamring and physician-scholar, regarded as founder of the Northern (byang) school of Tibetan medicine.

name: Zurkhar Nyamnyi Dorje (zur mkhar mnyam nyid rdo rje)
summary: Founder of the Zur school of Tibetan medicine.

name: Zurkhar Lodrö Gyalpo (zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po)
summary: Physician-scholar of the Zur school, author of the Oral Instructions of the Ancestors (mes po'i zhal lung), who also examined the question whether the Four Tantras is the Buddha's word.

name: Desi Sangye Gyatso (sde srid sangs rgyas rgya mtsho)
summary: Regent of the Fifth Dalai Lama's government, scholar of medicine and astronomy; author of the Blue Beryl commentary, the Supplement to the Oral Instructions and the history of medicine (Khogbug); he commissioned the medical paintings and founded the Chakpori medical college in Lhasa (1696).

name: Deumar Geshe Tenzin Phuntsok (de'u dmar dge bshes bstan 'dzin phun tshogs)

scholarly.text: b. 1672 or 1673 (as recalled); active early 18th c.

summary: Eighteenth-century physician and author of the materia medica 'Crystal Mirror and Crystal Rosary'.

name: Khyenrab Norbu (mkhyen rab nor bu)
summary: Physician to the Thirteenth Dalai Lama and first head of the Mentsikhang (institute of medicine and astrology) founded in Lhasa in 1916.

name: Vairocana, the translator (bai ro tsa na)
summary: In Sowa Rigpa's account the translator who brought the Four Tantras from India (via Kashmir) and taught them to Yuthok the Elder and to King Trisong Detsen before they were concealed as treasure.

name: Jamgön Kongtrul Lodrö Thayé ('jam mgon kong sprul blo gros mtha' yas)
places: Tsadra Rinchen Drak (Kunzang Dechen Ösel Ling)

realization_account.text: Regarded as an emanation of the translator Vairocana.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Co-founder of the Rimé movement. Born to a family with Bön connections, trained at Shechen and at Palpung, he received and practised the transmissions of all schools and compiled them in the Five Treasuries — the Treasury of Knowledge, the Treasury of Kagyu Mantra, the Treasury of Precious Treasures, the Treasury of Instructions and the Treasury of Extensive Teachings — mapping Tibetan practice as eight great chariots of practice lineages. He presented the other-emptiness view as the Great Madhyamaka and revived the Shangpa, Chöd and Kālacakra instructions.

name: Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo ('jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse'i dbang po)

realization_account.text: Regarded as the mind-emanation of Jigme Lingpa and as an emanation of Mañjuśrī; holder of the seven transmissions (bka' babs bdun).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Co-founder of the Rimé movement. A monk of the Sakya (Ngor) tradition based at Dzongsar, he sought out and received the teachings of all schools from many masters, revealed treasures, and was regarded as the holder of the seven modes of transmission; he inspired and directed Kongtrul's and Loter Wangpo's collections.

name: Jamyang Loter Wangpo ('jam dbyangs blo gter dbang po)
summary: Sakya (Ngor) master and student of Khyentse Wangpo who compiled the Compendium of Sādhanas and the Compendium of Tantras and published the Lamdre explanations.

name: Khenpo Shenga (Shenphen Chökyi Nangwa, gzhan phan chos kyi snang ba)
summary: Scholar associated with Dzogchen monastery and the Derge colleges, whose annotations on the thirteen great Indian treatises shaped the Rimé-influenced monastic curriculum.

name: Shechen Gyaltsap Gyurme Pema Namgyal (zhe chen rgyal tshab 'gyur med pad+ma rnam rgyal)
notes: Catalogue holds works under his name (OpenPecha P000010, P000011, P000159, P000160).
summary: Nyingma master of Shechen, student of Mipham and teacher of Dilgo Khyentse, author of collected advice, praises and commentaries.

name: Jamyang Khyentse Chökyi Lodrö ('jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse chos kyi blo gros)
notes: Catalogue: OpenPecha P000139 is a biography of him.
summary: Twentieth-century Rimé master of Dzongsar, recognized as an activity-emanation of Khyentse Wangpo, teacher of many of the lamas who carried the non-sectarian transmissions into exile.
